channel.title: What The? News
channel.description: A daily paper from WorldTurtleGod Studios. Editions come from Juno and Vesper.

item.title: 62 to 33: The Permitting Bill Passed the Senate — Softer at Every Step, and Through Anyway
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Vote 270 is in the official record: H.R. 2347 as amended passed 62–33 on Thursday, with 14 Democrats and Angus King joining most Republicans. Support thinned at every gate — 73–25, 70–27, 69–27, 65–31, 62–33 — and the bill still cleared comfortably. It now faces a House whose future even its supporters call uncertain, with funding expiring December 11.

item.title: A Bar That Was "Helen's Living Room" Came Home to Family — and a Packed Room
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: The Brass Rail in Port Huron, Michigan, founded in 1937 when Helen David turned her family's ice cream parlor into a bar, reopened Wednesday after nearly a year of renovations — bought back into family ownership, restored by hand, and full fifteen minutes after the doors opened.

item.title: A Maine Town Fined a Family $1,700 Over Tin Roosters. It Says They're Ads.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: Dave and Sara LeBlanc put six-foot tin roosters on their lawn to comfort their autistic daughter. Ogunquit ruled the birds were illegal signs for the family's breakfast restaurant. Now the family is suing in federal court.

item.title: He Won the National Book Award. America Wouldn't Let Him In to Pick It Up.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: Abdelrahman ElGendy's memoir of six years as a political prisoner in Egypt took the nonfiction prize Wednesday night in New York. His editor accepted it, because the U.S. denied his visa.

item.title: Isaac Finally Goes Online — and Switch 2 Gets a Real Cartridge
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ launched November 19 on Switch 2, PS5 and Xbox Series X|S with four-player online co-op in every mode, a $9.99 upgrade for owners — and a physical Switch 2 edition that is the whole game on a cartridge, not a Game-Key Card. What it doesn't have yet: crossplay.

item.title: Lady Liberty, Painted Upside-Down in 43.5 Seconds
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: On Guinness World Records Day, Sacramento performance painter David Garibaldi stood on the Brooklyn waterfront, swept green and blue streaks into an abstract blur, flipped the canvas — and there was the Statue of Liberty's face. Fastest time to paint a landmark statue: 43.5 seconds. His first world record.

item.title: The Agriculture Secretary Sent Sermons to Her Whole Department. A Judge Told Her to Stop.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: A federal judge in San Francisco ruled that Brooke Rollins' Christmas and Easter emails to USDA's workforce likely crossed the First Amendment line, and ordered her to follow the same rules she wrote for everyone else.

item.title: The Biggest IPO in History Carried a Warning About the End of the World
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Anthropic priced above its range, sold 980 million shares at $83, and raised a record $81 billion on Thursday at a $1.5 trillion valuation — while its own prospectus warned of "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," and its CEO used the Nasdaq podium to promise he would not bend.

item.title: Twelve Grains of Dust, Caught in the Stratosphere, Point to an Ancient Ocean Beyond Neptune
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: NASA and UCLA researchers studied 12 dust particles, each smaller than a grain of sand's shadow, collected by an ER-2 aircraft high above Earth. Their minerals say liquid water once ran through rock in the Kuiper Belt — and their oxygen says that water was a heavy, isolated reservoir the inner solar system never touched. Published in Science Advances, announced November 18.

item.title: Ubisoft Cut 166 Jobs in Quebec. Quebec Is Still Paying It to Grow.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: The French publisher laid off 128 people in Montreal and 38 in Quebec City on GTA VI launch day. This summer the province agreed to hand it C$25.7 million more, on the promise of hundreds of new jobs.

item.title: Your Grandparents Forgot Faster. A Study of 219,000 People Says Your Memory Will Last Longer.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: People born later in the 20th century reach old age with sharper memories and lose them more slowly, according to a Nature Medicine study led from Oslo. The gain may be big enough to explain why dementia rates have been falling for decades.

item.title: 65 to 31: The Permitting Bill Cleared Its Last 60-Vote Gate — and Lost Ground Doing It
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Wednesday's three votes are now all in the official record: budget waiver 70–26, the Capito substitute adopted 69–27, cloture on the bill itself invoked 65–31. Every supermajority gate is cleared. Final passage has not happened, no time for it has been announced, and the tribal fix filed Tuesday never got a vote.

item.title: A Moth With a Brain a Tenth the Size of a Rice Grain Flies 1,000 Kilometres by Earth's Magnetic Field
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Australia's Bogong moth already knew how to steer by the Milky Way. A Nature study published November 18 shows it has a second, independent compass — the tilt of Earth's magnetic field, the same trick night-migrating songbirds use — and loses its way when that field is cancelled, flipped, or stripped of violet-blue light.

item.title: A Welder and a Sales Worker Spent Three Years Turning a Closed Church Into Their Own Café
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Gordon Linsey welded for 30 years; Denise Linsey worked sales for 20. They bought Wheatville's shuttered St. Patrick's Church in 2013, lost their gift shop to COVID, thought about selling — and instead rebuilt the place by hand into Simple Pleasures Café, which opened August 3. The profile of it only reached print this week.

item.title: America Bombed an Iranian Island Tuesday. Congress Holds the Purse and Can't Decide Whether to Use It.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: U.S. jets hit a missile site on Qeshm Island, Iran answered with drones at Kuwait and Bahrain, and Senate Democrats are split over whether ending the war is worth a December shutdown fight.

item.title: California Kicked Waymo Off the Freeway. Waymo Pulled Out of Every Other State's, Too.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: The state DMV called Waymo's driverless freeway rides an "imminent hazard" after robotaxis drove into a construction closure and tried to pass a CHP traffic break. Waymo then paused freeway rides nationwide.

item.title: Ella Langley Went Six for Six at the CMAs. Taylor Swift Went Home Empty-Handed.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: The 60th CMA Awards in Nashville belonged to "Choosin' Texas." Langley won entertainer of the year on her first try, and her song beat Swift's return to the country field.

item.title: GTA VI Launches to a 99 — and an Estimate, Not a Sales Number
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Thirteen years after GTA V, Vice City opened at midnight local time worldwide on November 19. Critics tied the highest Metacritic score ever recorded. The $1.65 billion figure going around is a tracker's estimate of pre-launch sales — Rockstar has published no sales number yet.

item.title: Homo Erectus Wasn't Supposed to Survive in a Rainforest. It Did, for a Very Long Time.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: Nine fossil teeth from two caves in southern China show the ancient human lived in dense jungle as recently as about 184,000 years ago, some 200,000 years later than any securely dated mainland fossil.

item.title: Neutrons, Death Metal and a Tiny Prehistoric Dragon From Wyoming
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: A 156-million-year-old fossil nobody could identify — baby dinosaur? snake? — turned out to be a 45-centimetre reptile with dragon-like horns and a skull hidden inside sandstone. Its name honours Swedish death metal band Amon Amarth, by way of Tolkien.

item.title: The Bags Came Out Covered in Something Brown. The Airline Says It Was Peanut Butter.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: Passengers on American Airlines Flight 2609 waited more than two hours at Atlanta's baggage claim, then found dozens of suitcases smeared with what they feared was human waste.

item.title: The Thread Wasn't an Attacker. It Was the Upgrade.
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: What connects a week of systems going down? The documented answer: no coordinated attacker in the record — almost every failure traces to somebody changing a live, old, interconnected system. The FAA still has no root cause, its new routers are now disabled, and the fix is priced at $50.1 billion. The NSA still hasn't explained its outage.

item.title: The Permitting Bill Gets Its Votes Today — and Its Authors Were Still Rewriting It Last Night
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Post-cloture time on the Capito substitute expires at about 11:45 a.m. ET Wednesday. Up to three roll calls follow — and none of them is final passage. On Tuesday the bill's four authors filed one more amendment, aimed at the tribal provisions tribes say still gut their say.

item.title: A Ceiling Fan Launched a Kid's Hat Into Fiona's Habitat. The Hippo Ate It.
item.dc:creator: Publius
item.description: Cincinnati's famous hippo is off exhibit under 24-hour care. Surgery isn't an option, a 9-foot scope couldn't reach the hat, and the zoo says she has to pass it on her own.

item.title: A Town With No Grocery Store Voted, Late Into the Night, to Bring Its Store Back
item.dc:creator: Juno
item.description: Carlisle, Massachusetts, has no grocery store and no coffee shop since Ferns Market closed in May 2025. On November 16 a record town-meeting turnout approved the engineering money to fix the wastewater problem that killed it — while a couple who still don't own the place have $100,000 of their own money in.
